title: Blood and water (John 19:31–37)
hook: a soldier pierces his side; the Fathers saw baptism and the Eucharist flow out

segments.voice: Yesterday, woman, behold thy son, and Mary given to the beloved disciple. Your line was he took her to his own. Who did you take in? Day five hundred thirty.

There's a detail on many crucifixes that's easy to walk past: a wound in the right side, under the ribs. Sometimes it's just a red line. Some old paintings show a thin stream running from it, caught in a cup by an angel. In the Divine Mercy image, two rays, one pale and one red, pour out from that same place. All of it comes from a single moment, after Jesus has already died, that John says an eyewitness swore to.
screen: `A WOUND IN THE SIDE.` → `TWO RAYS, PALE AND RED.` → `ONE MOMENT AFTER DEATH.`

segments.voice: It's Friday, the day of preparation, and the sabbath about to begin is, John says, a great sabbath day. The authorities don't want bodies on crosses over the holy day, so they ask Pilate to have the legs broken to hasten death. The soldiers break the legs of the two men crucified with Jesus. When they come to him, he's already dead. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "But one of the soldiers with a spear opened his side, and immediately there came out blood and water." John stops the story to swear to it: the one who saw it has given testimony, and his testimony is true, so that you also may believe. Why does it matter so much? Partly, it shows he was truly dead, against anyone who'd say otherwise. Partly, John sees scripture fulfilled: not a bone of him shall be broken, as with the Passover lamb, and from Zechariah, "They shall look on him whom they pierced." But the early Church saw more. Notice the Douay's word: opened. It follows the Latin. Saint Augustine noticed it too. He wrote that the evangelist chose the word opened because there the door of life was opened, from which the sacraments of the Church flowed out: water for baptism, blood for the Eucharist. And some of the Fathers added a picture from Genesis: as Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam, the Church was born from the side of Christ asleep on the cross. The Catechism repeats that image. That's why Catholics look so carefully at that wound.
screen: `NO BONES BROKEN.` · `A SPEAR OPENED HIS SIDE.` · `AUGUSTINE: THE DOOR OF LIFE.` · `THE CHURCH FROM HIS SIDE.` · then, large: `BLOOD AND WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the side. If there's a crucifix near you, look at it. If not, find an image on your phone, or simply picture one. Breathe slowly. Let your eyes go to the side, the wound under the ribs, traditionally on the right. Stay there. Don't analyze it. Just look, the way John says the world will look on him. If you pray, you can hold Zechariah's line, they shall look on him whom they pierced, and let that be the whole prayer. If you don't, simply look, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Blood and water. What flowed from Jesus's opened side on the cross, which the Church Fathers saw as baptism and the Eucharist. Today's word.
Your line: they shall look on him. Today, the next time you see a cross, on a wall, a necklace, a steeple, really look at it for one breath. Day five hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Catholics honor the pierced heart of Jesus on the Solemnity of the Sacred Heart, and some pray before the Divine Mercy image, whose two rays stand for the blood and water.

fork.setup: you're a Roman soldier. the other two men are still alive and you've broken their legs. the man in the middle seems already dead. what do you do?
options: open his side with a spear.
leave him and report to Pilate.
fork.reveal: they don't break his legs. a soldier opens his side with a spear, and immediately there came out blood and water.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gruesome detail.
what it means: proof he was dead, scripture fulfilled, and for the Church, the sacraments flowing from his side.
what a scholar hears: the Vulgate's aperuit ('opened') drew Augustine's 'door of life' reading (Tractates on John 120); the Eve-from-Adam's-side image appears in the Catechism (766).

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook drops 'almost any crucifix', 'most people walk past' and 'famous', and no longer says John saw it 'with his own eyes' (19:35 speaks of 'he that saw it'); the sabbath line now follows John 19:31; 'many of the Fathers' and 'many pray' softened to 'some'.
Augustine, Tractate 120.2 on 'aperuit' (opened) and the door of life from which the sacraments flowed: paraphrased. Confirm.
CCC 766 on the Church born from the pierced side of Christ (citing Sacrosanctum Concilium 5 and Ambrose). Confirm.
Divine Mercy image: two rays, pale and red, as described in St. Faustina's diary (Diary 299). Confirm.
Art detail: angels catching the stream from the wounds in chalices appear in many medieval and Renaissance crucifixions. Confirm.
The wound is traditionally on the right side; John does not specify which side. Keeper may want 'traditionally the right side'.
